matching.reasoningTemplate: Microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and neurological signs suggests TTP - do not transfuse platelets reflexively.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Chap. 120 pp.967-968 (TTP/HUS); Chap. 105 pp.800-801 (familial/atypical HUS); Chap. on cutaneous purpura p.450; oncologic-emergencies HUS p.638; blood-smear schistocytes p.~640
clinicalPearls: The thrombotic microangiopathies are unified by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA): thrombocytopenia plus fragmented red cells (schistocytes) on the smear, biochemical haemolysis (high LDH, high unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin) and microvascular thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.967).

TTP was classically described as a pentad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, renal failure, neurologic changes and fever; the full pentad is now seen less often because earlier diagnosis and treatment intervene before it evolves (Harrison 22e pp.967-968).
ADAMTS13 activity below 10% is diagnostic of TTP; the assay (activity level plus anti-ADAMTS13 antibody) is central to working up any MAHA (Harrison 22e p.968).

ADAMTS13 levels are generally normal in HUS, although they have occasionally been reported as decreased - so a normal ADAMTS13 does not exclude a thrombotic microangiopathy other than TTP (Harrison 22e p.968).
Schistocytes are red-cell fragments produced by physical disruption against intravascular platelet/fibrin strands or external forces, and are the morphologic hallmark of MAHA (Harrison 22e p.~640).
The Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test is negative in microangiopathic haemolysis, helping separate it from autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (Harrison 22e p.638).

TTP is more common in women than men, and is over-represented in HIV infection and in pregnancy; congenital ADAMTS13 deficiency (Upshaw-Schulman) may first declare itself during a first pregnancy (Harrison 22e p.968).

In a classic HUS presentation, a preceding episode of diarrhoea (often bloody) in a child points to Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 as the commonest, though not the only, cause (Harrison 22e p.968).

Atypical HUS is essentially a complement-alternative-pathway disease - driven by mutations in complement components/regulators (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46/MCP, CFI, THBD) or anti-factor-H antibodies - and clinical disease usually requires a trigger such as infection, so penetrance is incomplete (Harrison 22e pp.800-801).
harrison.pathophysiology: TTP arises from deficient or antibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is secreted by endothelium as ultra-large multimers; when these are not cleaved they persist and drive pathological platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing microvascular thrombi. ADAMTS13 deficiency alone is not sufficient - congenitally ADAMTS13-deficient individuals develop TTP only episodically, implying a second trigger. In HUS the dominant lesion is endothelial injury with deposition of fibrin in capillary/arteriolar walls, predominantly in the kidney; typical (diarrhoea-associated) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7, while atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the complement alternative pathway with consequent endothelial damage. The shared downstream picture is microvascular platelet/fibrin thrombi causing red-cell fragmentation (MAHA), consumption thrombocytopenia and end-organ ischaemia (Harrison 22e pp.967-968, 800-801).
additionalDifferentials: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) - also gives thrombocytopenia and microangiopathy, but a consumptive coagulopathy predominates with prolonged PT and often prolonged aPTT (Harrison 22e p.967)
Atypical/complement-mediated HUS (aHUS) as a distinct entity from TTP (Harrison 22e pp.800-801)
Monoclonal cryoglobulinaemia with intravascular thrombi (Harrison 22e p.450)
Malignant hypertension affecting the renal microvasculature (Harrison 22e - listed among renal-microvascular causes of MAHA)
infectionMimics: Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 gastroenteritis (and other enterohaemorrhagic strains) preceding diarrhoea-associated HUS (Harrison 22e p.968)
HIV infection, which is associated with a higher incidence of TTP (Harrison 22e p.968)
nonInfectiousMimics: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (distinguished by abnormal PT/aPTT and clotting-factor/fibrinogen consumption) (Harrison 22e p.967)
Drug-induced microangiopathy - immune-mediated (ticlopidine, possibly clopidogrel, quinine) or by direct endothelial toxicity (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, gemcitabine, mitomycin C) (Harrison 22e p.968)
Chemotherapy-/cancer-associated HUS (mitomycin and gemcitabine most often; also cisplatin, bleomycin, proteasome and VEGF inhibitors) (Harrison 22e p.638)
Malignancy-induced HUS from microvascular metastases or extensive marrow invasion (Harrison 22e p.638)
Bone-marrow / haematopoietic stem cell transplant-associated microangiopathy (Harrison 22e pp.638, 967)
Pregnancy/postpartum-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (including HELLP in the obstetric context) (Harrison 22e pp.967-968)
additionalInvestigations: ADAMTS13 activity level AND anti-ADAMTS13 inhibitor/antibody assay (activity <10% diagnostic of TTP) (Harrison 22e p.968)
PT and aPTT - characteristically NORMAL in TTP/HUS; abnormal results point toward DIC (Harrison 22e p.967)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test - negative in MAHA (Harrison 22e p.638)
Full blood count with platelet count and peripheral smear for schistocytes (Harrison 22e p.968)
Renal function / serum creatinine and urinalysis (haematuria, proteinuria, granular or hyaline casts in HUS) (Harrison 22e p.638)

Complement-regulatory gene testing (C3, CFB, CFH, CD46, CFI, THBD) and anti-factor-H antibody for suspected atypical HUS - though assigning pathogenicity to variants is difficult and no functional diagnostic assay is established (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801)
redFlags: New unexplained thrombocytopenia with MAHA is a haematologic emergency - TTP is devastating if not recognised and treated promptly (Harrison 22e p.968)
Plasma exchange should be initiated urgently on clinical suspicion without waiting for confirmatory ADAMTS13 results, and likewise re-initiated promptly on suspected relapse (Harrison 22e p.968)
Fluctuating neurologic abnormalities (especially headache and confusion) in the setting of MAHA suggest TTP (Harrison 22e p.450)
Persistently low ADAMTS13 carries a greater risk of ongoing sequelae including stroke (Harrison 22e p.968)
In cancer-/transfusion-associated HUS, severe hypertension, pulmonary oedema and rapid worsening of haemolysis and renal function can follow a blood or blood-product transfusion (Harrison 22e p.638)
harrison.prognosis: Plasma exchange transformed TTP outcomes, reducing mortality from roughly 85-100% to about 10-30%. Relapse is common: 25-45% of plasma-exchange-treated patients relapse within 30 days of apparent remission and 12-40% relapse late, with relapse more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at presentation. In diarrhoea-associated HUS roughly 40% of children need some dialysis but overall mortality is <5%; non-diarrhoeal HUS carries higher mortality (~26%). Untreated atypical HUS had acute-phase mortality up to ~15% with up to 50% progressing to end-stage renal disease, though spontaneous remission occurs and relapse is likely with re-exposure to a trigger. Cancer-/chemotherapy-associated HUS has a high case-fatality rate, with most patients dying within months (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801, 638).
pitfalls: Do not reflexively transfuse platelets in TTP - platelet transfusion may fuel further microvascular thrombosis and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding (principle, Harrison 22e Chap. 120).

Do not assume normal coagulation excludes a thrombotic microangiopathy: PT and aPTT are characteristically normal in TTP/HUS, whereas they are abnormal in DIC - use them to discriminate, not to exclude (Harrison 22e p.967).
A normal ADAMTS13 does not point to TTP; ADAMTS13 is usually normal in HUS, so the diagnosis there rests on the clinical picture and complement work-up (Harrison 22e p.968).

Atypical HUS is a diagnosis of exclusion; patients may be started on plasma exchange until ADAMTS13 returns and the diagnosis clarifies, even though plasma exchange has not been shown to change clinical outcomes in aHUS (Harrison 22e p.968).
Plasma infusion/exchange does not alter the course of typical HUS or aHUS except in the subgroup with anti-factor-H antibodies (Harrison 22e p.968).
Drug-induced microangiopathy may improve simply on withdrawing or reducing the offending endothelial-toxic agent, so reflexive long-term plasma exchange may be unnecessary (Harrison 22e p.968).

Cancer-associated HUS can present without an evident malignancy - in one series 35% had no apparent cancer when the syndrome appeared, and it may surface weeks to months after the last chemotherapy dose (Harrison 22e p.638).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal TTP/HUS severity score in this material. Functional stratification used: ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic of TTP and severe deficiency at presentation predicts relapse and worse sequelae. HUS is grouped clinically into diarrhoea-associated (typical, Shiga-toxin) HUS versus non-diarrhoea-associated/atypical (complement-mediated) HUS, which carries higher mortality. (No PLASMIC score is described in the source and none is asserted here.) (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801).
